analysis.one_liner: Moves large class action lawsuits into federal court, caps plaintiffs' lawyers' fees, and requires clearer settlement notices.
analysis.headline: The Senate Judiciary Committee reported the bill favorably and placed it on the Senate calendar, but the full Senate never voted on it before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would move large class action lawsuits — those with claims totaling over $2 million from class members in different states — out of state courts and into federal courts. Any single defendant, or even a class member, could move the case to federal court without everyone's agreement. It also caps plaintiffs' lawyers' fees at a share of what the class actually recovers, requires settlement notices in plain language that disclose the lawyers' fees, and gives state attorneys general and the Justice Department 120 days' notice before a settlement can be approved.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses facing class action lawsuits, which would gain the right to move cases out of state courts — where they often fare worse — and into federal courts. Class members would get clearer notices and disclosure of attorney fee requests, and state attorneys general would get a chance to review settlements before they are approved.

how_it_helps.text: Gives federal courts jurisdiction over class actions where the combined claims of class members exceed $2 million and any class member or defendant is from a different state, and allows any single defendant — or any non-named class member — to move a state-court class action to federal court without the consent of the other parties.

Caps the fees and expenses awarded to class action plaintiffs' lawyers at a reasonable percentage of damages actually paid to the class, future financial benefits from stopped misconduct, and defendants' costs of complying with injunctions or settlements.

Requires that settlement notices to class members be written in plain, easily understood language, state the benefits of the settlement and the rights members give up, and disclose the dollar amount of attorney fees class counsel will seek.

Requires class lawyers to notify the attorney general of every state where class members live, plus the U.S. Attorney General, within 10 days of a proposed settlement, and bars a final-approval hearing until at least 120 days after that notice; class members in states left out of the notice could refuse to be bound by the settlement.

Directs the Judicial Conference of the United States to report to Congress within 12 months on best practices for making class settlements fair to class members and for making sure class members, not their lawyers, are the primary beneficiaries.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations defending against class actions would lose their ability to keep cases in state courts, and plaintiffs' attorneys would see their fee awards limited; class members whose claims ride on state law could find their cases pushed into a federal system that is generally less welcoming to state-law class claims.
analysis.who_pays_short: Class action plaintiffs' attorneys and state-court plaintiffs

drawbacks.text: Moving class actions to federal court primarily changes the forum in defendants' favor: federal courts are generally less receptive to state-law class claims, so cases that could have won meaningful recoveries in state court would become harder to bring or settle. The bill's own carve-outs also skip securities cases and internal corporate governance disputes entirely.

Capping lawyers' fees at a percentage of what the class actually receives, and allowing lodestar-based awards instead, could reduce the incentive for attorneys to take on large, expensive, risky cases against well-funded corporate defendants — leaving legitimate class claims without counsel.

The committee's work was contested: when the Judiciary Committee filed its written report, additional and minority views were filed alongside it, and the bill drew only one Democratic cosponsor among seven.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill packages real consumer protections — plain-language notices, fee disclosure, state attorney general review — around a jurisdiction change whose main effect is to move class actions to a forum friendlier to corporate defendants. The notice improvements are modest and could have been adopted without the federal-court transfer, which is the core of the bill and the reason business groups backed it. On balance, the bill's principal beneficiaries would have been corporate defendants, with class members receiving real but secondary benefits and bearing the risk of losing access to state courts.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee, was placed on the Senate's calendar of business, and then sat there — the full Senate never debated or voted on it before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Senator Chuck Grassley introduced the bill in February 1999 with seven cosponsors — six Republicans and one Democrat — and it was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
The Judiciary Committee held hearings in May 1999, marked the bill up in June 2000, and on July 27, 2000 reported it favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute.

The reported version raised the federal jurisdiction threshold from $75,000 to $2 million in aggregated claims and replaced a provision making sanctions mandatory for frivolous lawsuits with a directive that the Judicial Conference study class action settlements.
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders on July 27, 2000, but the Senate never took it up, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2001 with no floor vote ever held.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Plaintiffs' class action lawyers and corporate defendants both stayed with the status quo: businesses never got the federal-court exit, and class action attorneys kept their fee arrangements and forum leverage. Class members gained nothing either, since the notice improvements died with the bill.

against.name: Plaintiffs' trial lawyers (class action bar)
against.role: Attorneys who represent consumers in class action lawsuits
against.what_they_did: Opposed class action legislation that would move cases to federal court and cap attorney fees, as they consistently did during the class action reform debates of this era.

sides.party_line_note: Six of the bill's seven cosponsors were Republicans; the lone Democratic cosponsor was Herb Kohl, the committee report carried minority views, and the bill died without a floor vote where any split could be measured.

industries.note: The bill would let any single defendant move a class action out of state court into federal court and would cap the fees that can be awarded to the lawyers suing them. That matters to ordinary people because state courts are generally more receptive to the state-law consumer claims most class actions rely on.

The bill caps their fees at a share of what the class actually collects and adds notice and disclosure duties, including publicly stating the dollar amount of the fees they will seek. Some of that discipline serves class members, but the fee limits could also deter lawyers from taking big, risky cases against corporations.

The bill would require class counsel to notify every state attorney general of proposed settlements covering their residents and to wait 120 days before a final-approval hearing, giving them a window to object to settlements that shortchange consumers.
